title: Replication and Sharding
oneLiner: Copy your data to survive failures and serve more reads, and split it to handle more writes and more data than one machine can hold.
keyTakeaway: Replication copies the same data to several machines for read capacity and availability, but async replicas lag behind and a failover (switching to a standby when the main machine dies) can lose the last writes. Sharding splits the data so each machine holds a part, and the shard key decides whether the load is even and which queries stay cheap.
explanation:
A single database server eventually runs out of something: read capacity, write capacity, disk, or simply luck, because one machine is one failure away from an outage. Replication and sharding are the two answers, and most large systems use both. Replication keeps full copies of the same data on several machines. Sharding (also called partitioning) splits the data so each machine holds only part of it.

Replicate for two reasons. Reads: most apps read far more than they write, so a few read replicas can take most of the traffic off the main server. Availability: if a machine dies, another one already has the data and can take over. The common setup is leader-follower: one leader accepts all writes and streams them to followers, which serve reads. Multi-leader lets several nodes (often one per region) accept writes and sync with each other, which helps writes in many regions but means two leaders can change the same row at once and the conflict must be resolved. Leaderless systems such as Dynamo and Cassandra send each write to several replicas directly and use quorums (requiring a minimum number of replicas to answer) so that reads overlap the replicas that took the latest completed write.

Replication can be synchronous or asynchronous. Synchronous means the leader waits for a replica to confirm before telling the client the write succeeded: no data is lost if the leader dies, but every write is as slow as that replica, and if it is down writes stop. Asynchronous means the leader confirms right away and replicas catch up later, usually within milliseconds, sometimes seconds under load. That lag causes the read-after-write problem in part 1: you save, read from a replica, and see your old data. A common fix is to read your own recent writes from the leader. Lag also means a failover can lose writes the leader confirmed but never shipped, which is why many databases run one synchronous replica and the rest async.

Replication doesn't help with writes, because every copy still has to apply every write, and it doesn't help when the data is bigger than one machine. That's what sharding is for: each shard holds a subset of the rows and takes the writes for them. The hard part is the shard key. Hashing the key spreads data evenly but scatters ranges across all shards. Ranges (by id, by date, by name) keep related rows together for range queries but can be uneven, and a range by time or by increasing id sends all new writes to one shard. And no shard key fixes a single hot key, like a celebrity with millions of followers; that needs caching or special handling for the hot key itself.

Sharding has real costs. A query that doesn't include the shard key has to ask every shard and combine the results. Joins across shards and transactions that touch rows on two shards are slow or unsupported, so you pick the shard key so that the common queries stay on one shard (for example, shard by user id so all of one user's data lives together). Resharding when you add machines means moving data while serving traffic. With hash mod N, going from N to N+1 shards moves about N/(N+1) of all keys, as part 2 shows. The Consistent Hashing lesson covers the technique that cuts that to about 1/(N+1).

In an interview, start without either: one database handles more than people expect. Add read replicas when reads are the bottleneck, and shard only when writes or data size require it, and then say what the shard key is and why.
